intro.headline: Hundreds of brands, decades apart, one safe harbor.
intro.lede: Japanese conglomerates owned the mass market in 1982. Chinese vendors and private-equity roll-ups own it now. Different flags, identical structural pressure. In both eras exactly one brand stood alone, and it is no longer there.

points.title: 1978 to 1991
points.body: Nine Japanese conglomerates held 55% or more of global Hi-Fi share by 1982. Specialty retail differentiated with esoteric brands. The aspirational tier sold $1M systems without a stretch.

points.title: 2014 to 2026
points.body: GoerTek, IAG, HSG and Cosonic consolidate the floor. Tweeter is gone, Magnolia is inside Best Buy, Krell closed and is reopening, B&O is public and at less than half its peak.

points.title: Bang & Olufsen, 2007/08
points.body: Peak revenue of about $853M, roughly $1.25B in 2026 dollars. You had to put in the work to acquire B&O, the audio equivalent of the Birkin bag. New management didn't recognise their beachhead and almost destroyed the brand.

deep.headline: History rhymes.
deep.lede: Hundreds of Brands, Decades Apart, One Safe Harbor. Two eras, the consolidation table, and why each of these facts matters to AGF.

items.title: Japanese conglomerates dominate global Hi-Fi
items.body: Sony · Matsushita (Technics) · Pioneer · Yamaha · Kenwood · JVC · Sansui · Onkyo · Aiwa held 55%+ of global Hi-Fi share by 1982, from entry-level to premium big-box tiers.

items.title: Specialty retail differentiates with esoteric brands
items.body: Tweeter, Magnolia Hi-Fi, Crutchfield, and regional independents used Bose as entry and built reputations on Polk, Boston Acoustics, Snell, Advent, EPI, JBL, Infinity, ADS — often PE/KE owned even then.

items.title: Aspirational tier: the "eff you money" customer
items.body: Krell, Wilson Audio, Quad, Magnepan, McIntosh, Mark Levinson, conrad-johnson, Audio Research, Threshold, Bryston — $1M+ systems were not a stretch.

items.title: Bang & Olufsen stood alone — peak ~$853M USD
items.body: Equivalent to ≈ $1.25B in 2026 dollars. You had to put in the work to acquire B&O — the audio equivalent of the Birkin bag.

items.title: Chinese vendors + global PE roll-ups dominate
items.body: GoerTek/Dynaudio · IAG (Mission, Quad, Audiolab, Wharfedale) · Marshall family + HSG (Jan 2025) · Cosonic/Beyerdynamic. Same shape as the Japanese wave, different flag.

items.title: US specialty chain collapse
items.body: Tweeter, et al. — bankrupt 2007, closed Dec 2 2008. Big-box channel replaced by Amazon, JD, Taobao, Media Markt, Elkjøp.

items.title: Survivors
items.body: Crutchfield (1974) still private — $230M revenue, 50 years in. Magnolia absorbed inside Best Buy. Regional independents survive via custom install.

items.title: Krell closes
items.body: Following the death of owner/CEO Rondi D'Agostino. Service resumes Mar 2025; son Kristofer awarded 70%+ Feb 2025. Dan D'Agostino — rebuilt under his own name — is selling $250K monoblocks into Dolby Atmos maximalists.

items.title: B&O publicly traded, struggling
items.body: FY2023/24 revenue $402M — down from the 2007/08 peak.

sections.title: Why This Matters
sections.lede: AGF is built on a premise that runs counter to the dominant industry narrative: **stereo is not dead — it has never been properly implemented.** Every major audio innovation of the past 20 years (Dolby Atmos, multi-channel upmixing, object-based audio) has treated stereo as a constraint to escape. AGF treats stereo as the destination, refined to its highest form.

items.title: The Sweet Spot Problem
items.body:
Stereo inherently creates a narrow optimal listening position — the "sweet spot." The entire home-theatre / multi-channel industry has responded by adding more speakers, more upmixing, and more processing to mask the limitation. This is brute force.

AGF's l'Art codec takes the opposite approach: **eliminate the sweet spot from the rendering equation** rather than drowning it in channels. The result is a stable, immersive stereo soundfield that persists anywhere in the room, with no additional speakers, no extra processing overhead, and no compromise to the artist's intended mix.

items.title: The Consolidation Opportunity
items.body:
Between 2000 and 2024, the audio industry underwent a wave of M&A that concentrated brands under corporate ownership — Samsung/Harman, B&O's restructuring, Bose's retreat, Sonos's locked-in ecosystem. These acquisitions **stranded premium brands inside corporate R&D silos** where the parent's incentives (scale, cross-sell, walled gardens) diverge from the enthusiast buyer's desires (openness, sound quality, build longevity).

AGF's thesis: assemble the fragments that the consolidators left behind. Not by acquisition — by building a platform that independent brands, artists, and venues can adopt.

items.title: Artist-First Economics
items.body:
The streaming era normalized a revenue split of fractions of a cent per play, controlled by labels and platforms. AGF's model inverts this: **artists own their stereo masters**, set their own virtual-ticket pricing, and retain a 50/50 split in perpetuity on broadcast-mixed performances — with the right to block any broadcast without cause.

The green room is not a metaphor: AGF's physical venues are designed so the consumer product is *discovered* through the artist and the venue, not pushed through a sales funnel.

items.title: Retail as Community
items.body:
Apple's sterile boutiques defined the premium retail playbook for 20 years. AGF's alternative: **a venue that is first a performing-arts space**, second a flagship for the brand. The Front of House (bar + stage) generates foot traffic via live performances. The Balcony serves pros. The Green Room — hidden, appointment-only — is where the consumer product lives.

This inverts the standard retail funnel: discover the community first, discover the product second. The hard part. The whole point.

sections.title: The thesis in three lines
sections.body:
AGF positions at the intersection of premium audio, proprietary codec technology, and artist-first content distribution. The opportunity is defined by three converging factors: **wave of audio-industry M&A consolidation** that has stranded premium brands under corporate umbrellas, **unaddressed consumer demand** for genuine community-oriented physical retail, and a **patented acoustic rendering stack** (l'Art) that eliminates the sweet spot — a problem the entire industry has accepted as unsolvable.

The thesis: consolidate the fragments, build the platform, and serve the artists.
